concepts.title: Equality as a Foundational Ideal of Political Theory
concepts.definition: Equality does not claim that all people are identical in talent or taste; it claims that every person deserves the same consideration and respect simply as a human being. Because humans alone can reason about their actions and speak for their interests, political theory treats equal moral worth as the starting point of justice.
concepts.key_idea: Difference in ability is not a licence for difference in dignity -- equal consideration is owed to every person.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps101.txt lines 1-90 (introduction, human uniqueness of reason and language, equality as basic premise of political theory)
question_patterns: what does equality mean in political theory
in class 11 political theory: why is equality called a foundational ideal
does equality claim that all people are identical
how do reason and language support the claim of equal worth
why should differences in talent not decide differences in respect
explain equality of consideration with an example

solution_steps.explain: People differ in skills, tastes and achievements, but the ideal of equality concerns their moral worth, not their sameness.
The capacities to reason and to communicate make every person a subject of respect rather than an object of use.
Institutions should give each person equal consideration -- one vote, equal legal protection, equal opportunity -- regardless of birth or wealth.

concepts.title: Natural and Social Inequalities
concepts.definition: Some inequalities arise from inborn differences of strength, intelligence or talent -- natural inequalities -- while others are manufactured by society through unequal access to wealth, education and power -- social inequalities. Political theory worries mainly about the second kind, since they are humanly created and can therefore be humanly removed.
concepts.key_idea: Born differences need not become social hierarchies -- the arrangements we build decide whether they do.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps101.txt lines 90-170 (distinction between natural and social inequalities, examples of caste and gender hierarchy, whether inequalities are inevitable)
question_patterns: distinguish natural inequalities from social inequalities
in class 11 equality chapter: why are social inequalities considered unjust
are inequalities inevitable in any society
how does caste illustrate socially created inequality
can natural differences justify political dominance
give examples of inequalities produced by unequal access to education

solution_steps.explain: Ask whether a given gap in life chances comes from bodily or mental differences among people or from the way institutions distribute resources.
Social inequalities trace back to laws, customs and economic arrangements that people made and can remake.
Because societies can redesign their arrangements, social inequality is a matter of justice rather than fate.

concepts.title: Three Dimensions of Equality: Political, Social and Economic
concepts.definition: Equality operates on three linked fronts. Political equality grants each adult an equal vote and equal right to hold office; social equality rejects status hierarchies of caste, religion and gender in everyday life; economic equality asks that wealth differences not be so extreme that they swallow the other two.
concepts.key_idea: One vote and one law mean little if caste still stigmatises or wealth still commands -- the three equalities need each other.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps101.txt lines 170-260 (dimensions of equality, political social and economic equality, why formal equality alone is insufficient)
question_patterns: explain the three dimensions of equality with examples
in class 11 equality chapter: how are political and economic equality connected
why is social equality necessary for meaningful political equality
what does economic equality demand and how much
give an example where formal equality fails without economic equality
which dimension does universal adult franchise realise

solution_steps.explain: Universal adult franchise, equal candidacy and equal legal standing realise political equality.
Access to temples, wells, schools and public spaces without discrimination realises social equality.
Some levelling of wealth and income is needed so that the political and social rights of the poor are not hollow.
Each dimension reinforces the others; weakness in one leaks into and undermines the rest.

concepts.title: Equality of Opportunity and Natural Rights
concepts.definition: Equality of opportunity demands that positions and prizes go to effort and talent rather than birth, which requires at least a fair starting line for all. The related liberal claim of natural rights holds that every person possesses certain rights -- life, liberty and the like -- before and above any government, which no ruler may cancel.
concepts.key_idea: Fair competition needs fair starting points, and rights that precede the state protect the competitor.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps101.txt lines 260-350 (equality of opportunity, affirmative action debate, natural rights and their role in liberal thought)
question_patterns: what does equality of opportunity require in practice
in class 11 equality chapter: how do natural rights support equality
why is a level starting field part of equal opportunity
do natural rights exist before the state is formed
how can unequal help for disadvantaged groups serve equal opportunity
distinguish equality of opportunity from equality of outcome

solution_steps.explain: Jobs, offices and honours must be open to all comers and decided by relevant merit, not by birth or patronage.
Minimum education, health and livelihood conditions must be secured, or the race is lost before it begins.
Natural rights to life, liberty and free expression protect the arena in which equal opportunity can operate.

concepts.title: Equality in the Indian Constitution
concepts.definition: The Indian Constitution weaves equality through its fabric: Articles 14 to 18 promise equality before law, ban untouchability and titles, and guarantee equal public access; Article 15 and 16 permit special provisions for disadvantaged groups; and directive principles push toward reducing economic concentration.
concepts.key_idea: Formal equality plus enabling provisions for the disadvantaged -- the Constitution treats equality as a project, not just a rule.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps101.txt lines 350-430 (equality provisions of the Indian constitution, Articles 14 to 18, provisions for disadvantaged groups and reservations)
question_patterns: which articles of the Indian constitution deal with equality
in class 11 equality chapter: how does the constitution balance equality with special provisions
what does equality before law mean under Article 14
why did the constitution abolish untouchability and titles
how do reservations reconcile with the ideal of equality
which directive principles aim at economic equality

solution_steps.explain: Articles 14 to 18 install equality before law, ban discrimination, outlaw untouchability and abolish titles.
Special provisions, including reservations, are allowed for socially and educationally backward groups as instruments of real equality.
Directive principles direct the state to spread resources and reduce concentration of wealth, carrying equality into the economy.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student says that because some people are naturally stronger, rule by the strong is justified. Evaluate the argument using the natural and social inequality distinction.

solution_template.explain: The argument treats a natural difference in strength as a title to political power.
Even granting bodily differences, turning them into rulership is a social arrangement, chosen and changeable.
Equal moral worth bars converting any natural advantage into permanent dominance; political equality remains the defensible position.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Two villages deny a Dalit family access to the public well. Which constitutional provisions are violated and how does the state respond?

solution_template.explain: Equal access to public wells, roads and bathing places is guaranteed, and untouchability in any form is abolished.
Denying well access on caste grounds violates both the equality articles and the abolition of untouchability.
Law punishes such practices and protective provisions empower the state to act for the excluded group.
